title: How far is the laddu when it sits on an edge?
description: A cube has side six centimetres, with an ant at the centre of the front face and a laddu at the middle of the edge between the top face and the right face. The board unfolds the right face beside the front face and finds the slanted line with the right triangle rule. Keeko's doubt is that the path is nine centimetres.
teaching_notes: One idea: unfold so both places lie on one flat sheet, then the shortest path is a slanted straight line whose length comes from a right triangle. Watch for students who add the across and up distances instead.

source: A cube has side 6 cm. An ant is at the centre of the front f
video_script.why: The child finds the shortest path to a laddu on an edge by unfolding the right face beside the front face and using the right triangle rule, because the straight line on the flat sheet is slanted.
video_script.substitution: cube of side 6 cm; right face unfolded beside the front face; laddu 3 + 3 = 6 cm across and 3 cm up from the ant; path = square root of (6 x 6 + 3 x 3) = square root of 45, about 6.71 cm.
video_script.anchor: the cube of the book with the ant and the laddu on an edge, the right face unfolded beside the front face
video_script.wrong_answer: the ant goes up three and then across six, so the path is nine centimetres
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds the up distance 3 and the across distance 6 to get 9 cm; that path turns a corner on the flat net, and the straight line cutting across it is shorter, about 6.71 cm, so the doubt is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The shortest path is about six point seven one centimetres, a slanted straight line

final_answer.value: About 6.71 cm, a slanted straight line on the net
final_answer.spoken: about six point seven one centimetres, a slanted straight line on the net

names.{{NAME_1}}: the theorem used for the shortest path of 40 cm

hold_back: About 6.71 cm, a slanted straight line on the net
maths_rules: a path on the cube and the matching path on the net have the same length
unfold the right face flat beside the front face; the laddu on the edge is on the right face, 3 cm from the shared edge, level with the top
from the ant at the centre of the front face: 3 cm to the shared edge + 3 cm beyond it = 6 cm across; from half height to the top edge = 3 cm up
right triangle with sides 6 and 3: path squared = 6 x 6 + 3 x 3 = 36 + 9 = 45
path = square root of 45, about 6.71 cm
wrong idea: up 3 then across 6 = 9 cm, a path that turns a corner and is longer than the slanted line
video_script.design: One idea: unfold, draw the slanted line, and use the right triangle. The right face swings flat beside the front face; the slanted line is drawn in the accent colour and the nine centimetre route in the warning colour.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about an ant and a laddu on a cube.
<bookmark mark='cube'/>The cube has side six centimetres, and the ant is at the centre of the front face.
<bookmark mark='laddu'/>The laddu is at the middle of the edge between the top face and the right face.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>The ant can walk only on the surface. Find the shortest path.

narration: <bookmark mark='net'/>A net means a flat shape that folds into the solid.
<bookmark mark='line'/>On the net, the shortest path between two places is a straight line. It keeps its length on the cube.
<bookmark mark='edge'/>The laddu sits on an edge, so it belongs to two faces at once.

narration: <bookmark mark='across'/>Step two, measure the gap. The ant is three centimetres from the shared edge, and the laddu is three centimetres beyond it. That is six centimetres across.
<bookmark mark='up'/>The ant is at half the height, and the laddu is at the top. The laddu is three centimetres up.

narration: <bookmark mark='tri'/>Step three, the straight line is the longest side of a right triangle with sides six and three.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>The {{NAME_1}} Theorem applies to a right triangle. It says the square of the longest side is the sum of the squares of the other two.
<bookmark mark='work'/>Six times six is thirty six, and three times three is nine. Thirty six plus nine is forty five. The path is the square root of forty five.
